statement: Ana makes hollow square frames, one tile wide, from square tiles. The first three have 3, 5 and 7 tiles along each side. She keeps going. How many tiles does the next frame need?

choices.misconception: I counted 9 tiles along the top and bottom and 8 down each side, so one corner on each side was counted twice.
I counted 9 tiles on each of the 4 sides, so every corner tile was counted twice.
I counted 9 tiles on each of the 4 sides and then added the 4 corner tiles again.
I counted a full 9 by 9 square and forgot the frame is hollow.

hints: How many tiles along each side does the next frame have?
The sides grow 3, 5, 7, so the next frame has 9 tiles along each side. Count the tiles in a frame carefully: each corner tile belongs to two sides, so count it only once.
The frames have 8, 16 and 24 tiles. Each new frame adds the same number of tiles. Or count the 9-tile frame directly: top, bottom, then the tiles left on each side.

solutions.reliable: The sides go 3, 5, 7, growing by 2 each time, so the next frame has 9 tiles along each side. Count it: 9 tiles on the top and 9 on the bottom. Each side then needs only 7 more tiles, because its two corner tiles are already counted. That is $9 + 9 + 7 + 7 = 32$ tiles. Check with the pattern: the frames have 8, 16 and 24 tiles, adding 8 each time, and $24 + 8 = 32$. The idea to keep: corner tiles belong to two sides, so count them only once.
solutions.elegant: Count 4 sides of 9 tiles, which is 36, then take away the 4 corner tiles that were counted twice: $36 - 4 = 32$.

whyOnTest: Growing frames test whether corner tiles are counted once, and the classic trap of four times the side double-counts every corner.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
